title: Aurora Studios: leaving the data centre
prompt: Our client is Aurora Studios, a national broadcaster whose streaming platform runs in two company-owned data centres, Ashvale and Derrow. The hardware in both sites is approaching end of life, and a full refresh is due next year. Before committing that money, the board wants to know whether Aurora should instead migrate the platform to a public-cloud provider. They have asked us to compare the two paths over the next five years and recommend one.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 1 — Owned data centres: annual cost and installed capacity
exhibits.unitsNote: Costs recur every year of the five-year horizon

exhibits.title: Exhibit 2 — The hardware refresh
exhibits.text: If Aurora keeps the data centres, the end-of-life hardware in both sites must be replaced next year at a one-off cost of $200M. The refresh does not change either site’s capacity or annual fixed cost.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 3 — Average demand vs installed capacity by site
Exhibit 4 — The cloud offer, key terms
exhibits.unitsNote: A cloud server unit delivers the same workload as one owned server unit

rows: Price per server unit per year
One-off migration cost (incl. one year of dual running)

questions.prompt: Before we build the comparison, what should we clarify with Aurora first? Select the two most relevant.
options: How many subscribers has the streaming platform added in each of the last five years?
What does the platform run on today, and what would staying put actually cost?
Does the board have a specific financial objective or constraint for this decision?
Which production studios and back catalogues does Aurora own?
What is the advertising revenue per hour of viewing?

optionRationale: Subscriber growth would matter for a revenue case; this one turns on the cost of serving a platform whose demand is already given.
The baseline. You cannot compare against "staying" until you know what staying costs and what it commits Aurora to.
A must-have. Almost every invest-or-migrate case has a hurdle — a saving target or a budget cap — that the answer is measured against.
Content assets sit on the revenue side of the business and do not bear on where the platform is hosted.
Advertising economics are identical in both scenarios — viewers cannot tell where the stream is served from.
commonMistakes: Reaching for revenue-side data — subscribers, advertising — in a decision where revenue is identical on both paths
Skipping the objective, which is what the whole comparison is later judged against

questions.followUp:
The platform serves 30 million registered viewers from the two sites, Ashvale and Derrow, and both are run by Aurora’s own engineering team.

On objectives: the board wants the cheaper path over the next five years, and it will only migrate if the move saves at least $150M over that horizon — it will not trade reliability for a marginal saving.

questions.prompt: Which areas would you investigate to compare the two paths? Select the four most relevant.
options: The full five-year cost of staying: annual operating costs plus the hardware refresh
How cloud pricing maps onto Aurora’s actual demand — what it would really pay for
The one-off cost and disruption of migrating a platform that must stay live
Which presenters front Aurora’s flagship programmes
How Aurora’s programme budget is allocated across genres
The risks of each path — reliability, vendor lock-in, and the capability to run either
What the original construction of the two data centres cost a decade ago

optionRationale: One whole side of the comparison — and the refresh is the reason the decision is live now.
The other side. Cloud economics depend entirely on how much capacity Aurora must pay for, which is not the same as what it built.
Migration is not free, and for a live broadcast platform the execution cost and risk belong in the base case, not a footnote.
Talent contracts sit on the content side and are untouched by where the platform is hosted.
Programme mix does not change the infrastructure bill.
Always in an initial structure — and here the risk profile of the two paths differs more than their cost.
Sunk cost. What the sites cost to build says nothing about what to do next.
commonMistakes: Loading the structure with content-side questions the decision cannot touch
Treating migration as free and comparing only the run-rate costs

questions.followUp:
On demand: streaming is spiky. The platform is built for Saturday-night peaks, so the data centres carry far more capacity than an ordinary day uses — and Aurora pays to power and maintain all of it. The cloud is priced differently: you pay for what you reserve, not for what you built.

On capability: Aurora has never run a cloud workload at scale. The engineering team’s entire experience is on-premise.

questions.prompt: Which data points do you need to compare the five-year cost of staying against the five-year cost of migrating? Select five.
options: Annual fixed cost of each data centre
The original purchase price of the current servers
The one-off cost of the hardware refresh
The cloud price per unit of capacity
Aurora’s annual programme production budget
The capacity the cloud contract would require Aurora to reserve
The one-off cost of the migration itself
The advertising rates Aurora charges

optionRationale: The run-rate of the staying path; five years of it is most of that side of the ledger.
Sunk. What the old hardware cost has no bearing on the forward comparison.
The one-off on the staying side, and the piece people forget because it has not been paid yet.
Half of the cloud run-rate calculation.
Content spend is identical on both paths and cancels out of the comparison.
The other half of the cloud run-rate: the bill is price × reserved capacity, not price × installed capacity.
The one-off on the cloud side, and it includes keeping both environments alive during cutover.
Revenue-side, identical in both scenarios.
commonMistakes: Reaching for sunk or content-side figures in a forward-looking cost comparison
Taking the cloud price but forgetting you also need the reserved capacity to multiply it by

questions.followUp:
That gives you both sides of the comparison:

staying = (annual data-centre cost × 5) + hardware refresh
cloud = (annual cloud bill × 5) + migration cost
annual cloud bill = reserved capacity × price per server unit

Here is what the two data centres cost to run, and what the refresh would come to.

questions.prompt: Exhibits 1 and 2 give the cost of keeping the platform in Aurora’s own data centres. What is the total five-year cost of staying?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter in $ millions, rounded to the nearest million.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Annual fixed cost: $70M + $50M = $120M.
Five years: $120M × 5 = $600M.
Plus the one-off refresh: $600M + $200M = $800M.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the refresh and answering $600M — the hardware does not survive the horizon
Multiplying the refresh by five; it is a one-off
Adding the capacity figures into the cost line — the K-unit column is capacity, not dollars

questions.followUp:
Staying costs $800M over the five years, $120M a year of it just to keep the lights on.

Now the cloud side — starting with how much capacity Aurora actually needs. The sites were sized for the biggest broadcast nights of the year, not for an ordinary Tuesday.

questions.prompt: Exhibit 3 shows average demand against installed capacity at each site. On an average day, what share of Aurora’s total installed capacity is actually in use?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter as a percentage to one decimal place — for 42.5%, type 42.5.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Average demand: 8K + 4K = 12K server units.
Installed capacity: 20K + 12K = 32K server units.
Utilisation: 12 / 32 = 37.5%.
commonMistakes: Reading one site instead of both
Inverting the ratio and answering 267%
Averaging the two sites’ utilisation rates (40% and 33%) without weighting by size

questions.followUp:
Right — nearly two thirds of what Aurora built sits idle on an average day (62.5%, to be exact), and every idle unit is powered, cooled and maintained anyway.

The cloud prices the same workload differently. Here are the terms Aurora has been offered.

questions.prompt: Using the cloud terms in Exhibit 4 and the demand figures in Exhibit 3, what would Aurora’s annual cloud bill be?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter in $ millions, rounded to the nearest million.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Reserved capacity: average demand of 12K units × 1.25 = 15K server units.
Annual bill: 15,000 units × $6,000 = $90M.
commonMistakes: Reserving installed capacity (32K units) instead of demand plus headroom — that is the mistake the cloud model exists to fix
Forgetting the 25% headroom and answering $72M
Slipping a factor of a thousand between K units and dollars

questions.followUp: A $90M bill against $120M of data-centre fixed cost — $30M a year in Aurora’s favour. But the annual gap is not the decision: the migration itself costs money, and the refresh only bites if Aurora stays.

questions.prompt: What is the total five-year cost of the cloud path, including the migration?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter in $ millions, rounded to the nearest million.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Annual bill: $90M × 5 = $450M.
Plus the one-off migration: $450M + $150M = $600M.
commonMistakes: Adding the $200M hardware refresh to the cloud path — migrating is precisely how Aurora avoids it
Charging the migration cost every year; it is a one-off
Adding an extra year of data-centre cost for dual running — the $150M already includes it

questions.followUp: So the cloud path comes to $600M all-in over the same five years.

questions.prompt: The board said it would only migrate for a saving of at least $150M over five years. How large is the saving the migration actually delivers?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter in $ millions, rounded to the nearest million.

commonMistakes: Comparing only the run-rates ($120M vs $90M a year) and reporting $150M — the one-offs are where the paths differ most
Netting the refresh out of both sides; only the staying path pays it
Comparing the saving to the $150M migration cost instead of to the board’s objective

questions.followUp: A $200M saving clears the board’s $150M bar — and a full $200M refresh is what staying would have spent next year, which is why the decision cannot wait. The financial case is made; before recommending, we need the risks of a migration this size.

questions.prompt: What are the most relevant risks of migrating the platform to the cloud? Select the three most relevant.
options: Audience risk — viewers may drift away from Aurora’s programming
Capability risk — Aurora’s engineers have never run a cloud platform at scale
Vendor lock-in — once migrated, the provider’s future price rises are hard to escape
Cutover risk — an outage during migration on a platform that must stay live
Weather risk — storms damaging the two data centres

optionRationale: Programming taste has nothing to do with where the stream is served from; viewers cannot tell.
Real, and flagged earlier: the team’s whole experience is on-premise, and the operating model changes on day one.
Real, and structural: the five-year saving rests on the provider’s prices, which Aurora will be in a weak position to renegotiate once the data centres are gone.
Real, and the sharpest near-term threat: a broadcaster’s platform cannot go dark for a weekend while the migration happens.
The data centres are being left, not defended — and site weather risk exists equally today.
commonMistakes: Picking audience or weather risk out of habit rather than asking what the migration itself changes
Missing lock-in — the risk that the $200M saving quietly erodes after the point of no return

questions.followUp:
Lock-in: negotiate multi-year price caps and committed-use discounts now, while Aurora still has a credible alternative, and keep the platform portable where it is cheap to do so.

Capability: hire a core of cloud engineers, retrain the existing team, and lean on the provider’s migration support — this is a people plan, not just a technology plan.

Cutover: migrate service by service with the dual-running year the offer already pays for, rehearse the rollback, and move the crown-jewel live channels last.

questions.prompt: Aurora’s CFO joins your wrap-up call and asks for your recommendation on the migration. Please give your answer in seven to eight lines maximum.

keyPoints: Leads with the recommendation: migrate to the cloud
Gives the financial reason with numbers: $600M versus $800M over five years — a $200M saving against the board’s $150M bar
Explains why: Aurora pays for 32K units of capacity and uses 12K; the cloud charges for 15K
Notes the timing: the $200M refresh falls due next year, so deciding now is what makes the saving real
Names the conditions: price caps negotiated before signing, a capability plan for the engineering team, and a phased cutover with rollback
Keeps reliability explicit — the board said it would not trade it away, so the answer must say how it is protected
Stays inside seven or eight lines and does not narrate the calculation
commonMistakes: Walking the CFO through the arithmetic instead of leading with the answer
Presenting the migration as unconditionally good and omitting lock-in and cutover risk
Quoting the $30M annual gap as the saving and ignoring the one-offs on both sides

closing: That is the end of the case. Your transcript is ready — copy it into an LLM to be graded on what you actually said, not on what you meant.
